--- title: "Reaction networks and moment closure" course-unit: ch07-reaction-networks status: complete --- ## From states to flows We have written this same epidemic three times now — as an ODE right-hand side, as a drift and diffusion, as a pair of jumps. Three files, one model, and three chances to make a typo. - Writing **states changing** ties the model to one mathematical setting. - Writing **flows** — which events happen, at what rate, what each changes — does not. ::: {.notes} This is the one idea of the session, so do not let it pass as a style preference. Ask them what they would have to change to turn Monday's ODE into Tuesday's jump process: not the assumptions, not the parameters, only the notation — and yet it meant a rewrite each time, with a fresh opportunity for a sign error in every one. Nothing about the biology changes here: same SIR assumptions, same baseline parameters as the previous two sessions. ::: ## A flow is a rate and a change $$ S + I \xrightarrow{\ \kappa\ } 2I, \qquad I \xrightarrow{\ \gamma\ } R, \qquad \kappa = \beta c / N. $$ A **propensity** and a **stoichiometry**: how fast, and what changes. That pair is a *description*, not a simulation algorithm — which is why the representation becomes a choice you make at the end, not a commitment you make at the start. ::: {.notes} The deeper point is about *when* you commit. An ODE file has already decided that the state is continuous and the dynamics deterministic. A flow specification has decided neither, so the same object can answer a deterministic question in the morning and a stochastic one in the afternoon. Two arrows is the whole model. Say that out loud against the three files we have accumulated. ::: ## One specification, three models {.smaller} Read off the stoichiometry $V$ and the propensities $a(X)$: $$ V=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\1&-1\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad a=(\kappa SI,\ \gamma I)^\mathsf{T}. $$ | Lowering | Construction | |---|---| | ODE | $\dot X = Va(X)$ | | SDE | $dX = Va(X)\,dt + V\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{a})\,dW$ | | Jump | event $j$ at rate $a_j$, adding $V_{\cdot j}$ | | Moments | $d\,\mathbb{E}[X]/dt = V\,\mathbb{E}[a(X)]$ | You wrote this pair yesterday: ```julia MassActionJump(κ, [S => 1, I => 1], [S => -1, I => 1]) # ^ rate ^ gives a₁ ^ first column of V ``` ::: {.notes} Put the `MassActionJump` line up and say the thing plainly: the two lists you filled in yesterday were $a$ and $V$. Nothing about them was specific to jump processes. We called it a jump because that is what we then asked for, but the description itself never mentioned an algorithm. That is why the table has four rows and not three. The same $(V,a)$ that generates a Gillespie simulation also generates the drift and diffusion of the SDE — these are exactly the $V$ and $a$ from the stochastic differential equations session — and, as the rest of this session shows, the equations for the moments too. One description, four questions. ::: ## The same network, three solvers {.smaller} ::: {#cell-slide-ch06-lowerings .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using Catalyst, OrdinaryDiffEq, StochasticDiffEq, JumpProcesses, StableRNGs sir_network = @reaction_network begin κ, S + I --> 2I γ, I --> R end ps = [:κ => 0.05 * 10.0 / 1000, :γ => 0.25] tspan = (0.0, 40.0) ode = solve(ODEProblem(sir_network, [:S => 990.0, :I => 10.0, :R => 0.0], tspan, ps), Tsit5()) sde = solve(SDEProblem(sir_network, [:S => 990.0, :I => 10.0, :R => 0.0], tspan, ps), LambaEM(); seed = 20250906) jump = solve(JumpProblem(sir_network, [:S => 990, :I => 10, :R => 0], tspan, ps; aggregator = Direct(), rng = StableRNG(20250906)), SSAStepper()) round.((maximum(ode[2, :]), maximum(sde[2, :]), maximum(jump[2, :])); digits = 1) ``` ::: {#slide-ch06-lowerings .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (157.6, 165.8, 165.0) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.notes} Three peaks from one network, and no SIR equations were retyped between them. Worth pausing here: adding an exposed class would propagate to all three at once. That is the practical payoff, and it is what the worksheet starts from. ::: ## If it is mass action, use Catalyst {.smaller} The network above is **mass action**: each propensity is a rate constant times the reactants present. Assume that, and `Catalyst.jl` gives you three things that are otherwise separate pieces of work. | | what you get | |---|---| | **Compact** | one line per event; the arrow carries stoichiometry and rate law | | **Plural** | ODE, SDE, jump — and the CME — from the one object | | **Analysable** | the network is data, so packages can read it: conservation laws, and moment equations | `MomentClosure.jl` is the third of these, and it is the rest of this session: it takes the network itself, not your code, and derives equations from it. ::: {.notes} Be precise about what the mass-action assumption buys and what it costs. It costs you the freedom to write an arbitrary rate law — a saturating force of infection or an explicit delay is not a reaction, and then you are back in ModelingToolkit writing the equation yourself. Catalyst does allow custom rate expressions, but the moment the rate stops being mass action you also lose the automatic moment equations, which is the part that matters today. What it buys is that the model stops being code and becomes *data*. That is the enabling step for the third row: `MomentClosure` does not parse your Julia function, it reads the stoichiometry and propensities, which is only possible because the arrow told it both. Most of epidemiology is reactions — ageing, waning, vaccination, treatment — so this is a wide assumption, not a narrow one. ::: ## Why the moments do not close {.smaller} Exact equation for the mean: $$ \frac{d\,\mathbb{E}[X]}{dt}=V\,\mathbb{E}[a(X)]. $$ Recovery is linear, so $\mathbb{E}[\gamma I]=\gamma\mathbb{E}[I]$. Transmission is **bimolecular**: $$ \mathbb{E}[\kappa SI]=\kappa\big(\mathbb{E}[S]\mathbb{E}[I]+\operatorname{Cov}(S,I)\big). $$ - First moments need second moments, second need third, and so on. - The ODE *is* the approximation that drops $\operatorname{Cov}(S,I)$. ::: {.notes} This finally explains an observation from the jump-process session: the ensemble mean does not lie on the ODE curve. The covariance between S and I is strongly negative during an epidemic, so the ODE peak sits above the ensemble mean. It is a bias, not sampling error, and it does not shrink by running more trajectories. ::: ## Closure: cut the hierarchy off - Keep moments to order $m$; express higher ones via an assumed distribution. - **Normal closure**: set third central moments to zero. - The assumption is about the *shape of the distribution*, not the model. ::: {#cell-slide-ch06-closure .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using MomentClosure raw = generate_raw_moment_eqs(sir_network, 2) closed = moment_closure(raw, "normal") (equations = length(equations(raw.odes)), closure = "normal") ``` ::: {#slide-ch06-closure .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (equations = 9, closure = "normal") ``` ::: ::: ::: {.notes} Nine equations at order two: three means and six second moments. Stress that this is an uncontrolled approximation — there is no step size to refine that guarantees convergence, unlike everything else in the course so far. ::: ## Two routes to the scatter {.smaller} We want more than a mean: we want the *spread* of outcomes. There are two ways to get it. | | ensemble of simulations | moment equations | |---|---|---| | What you solve | $M$ exact trajectories | one system of 9 ODEs | | Set-up | none | derive and compile, once per model | | Each query | $M \times$ events, and events grow with $N$ | independent of $M$ and of $N$ | | Accuracy | exact, up to Monte Carlo error | biased by the closure assumption | | To halve the error | run $4M$ trajectories | nothing you can turn | Monte Carlo error falls as $1/\sqrt{M}$, so precision is bought in quadruplicate. Closure has no such dial — and no such cost. ::: {.notes} The last row is the honest asymmetry and it cuts both ways. With an ensemble you always know how to do better: run more. It costs four times the compute for two times the precision, but it is a knob, and it converges to the truth. Closure has no knob at all. There is no step size to refine, no trajectory count to raise; the bias from assuming a shape is simply there. So it is not that closure is a cheap approximation to simulation — it is a different kind of answer, one you must validate against simulation at least once before you trust it in a regime where you cannot afford to simulate. Be fair about the set-up row: deriving and compiling the moment equations takes a couple of seconds, which is real but paid once per model. What you buy is that every subsequent solve is essentially free, and that is the property that matters when the model sits inside a sweep or a likelihood. ::: ## Does it match an ensemble? {.center .smaller} ::: {#cell-fig-slide-ch06-closure .cell execution_count=1} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: {#fig-slide-ch06-closure .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` Infectious prevalence: mean and one standard deviation from 200 jump trajectories (band) against the normal moment closure (lines), with the wall-clock cost of each route. ::: ::: ::: {.notes} Nine equations reproduce what two hundred simulations found, for both the centre and the width of the distribution, and the two timings in the title are the argument. Let them read the gap themselves rather than announcing it. Say what the timings do and do not include, because someone will ask. Both sides are warmed up, so this compares the cost of asking the question again, not of asking it the first time. Deriving and compiling the moment equations took a couple of seconds before the clock started; the ensemble had one trajectory run to compile the stepper. After that the ratio is about four thousand to one, and it widens with N, because trajectory cost follows the event count while the nine equations do not know how big the population is. Then be careful about what has been shown. This is one network, at one population size, in a regime where the epidemic is large and extinction is not in play. It is evidence that the closure works *here*, which is exactly the validation the previous slide said you must do once. The next slide is where it stops working. ::: ## When closure fails - Ask for a log-normal closure on this network and the solver cannot even start. - Closures degrade where stochasticity matters most: **small counts**, early outbreak, near extinction. - A closure describes the ensemble, never a single outbreak — it cannot give you the probability of fade-out. ::: {.notes} Show the failure rather than hiding it. A log-normal shape is untenable for a compartment that reaches zero. The rule to leave them with: always check the return code, and always compare against simulation before trusting a closure. ::: ## Takeaways - Write **flows**, not states: the representation becomes a choice at the end. - Mass action means Catalyst can read the model as data, not as code. - The moment hierarchy does not close because transmission is bimolecular. - Closure buys the spread without the ensemble: no $1/\sqrt{M}$ to pay, but a bias you cannot refine away and must check against simulation once. - Mass action is still an assumption; contact structure needs the individual level. ::: {.notes} Next session is sensitivity and identifiability. The link is direct: cheap ensemble statistics make it feasible to sweep parameters without running a full simulation study at every point. :::
